opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think we're looking at the same underlying problem from two different angles.

The problem is the standard residual connection. In a Transformer, each layer's output just gets added to the stream, with equal weight, layer after layer. It's simple and it made deep networks trainable, but it's also rigid. By the time you're forty or eighty layers deep, the information from early layers is diluted in one big sum. A later layer can't really say, "I specifically want what layer five computed." It only sees the mixture.

As I understand it, the attention residual idea attacks this directly. Instead of a fixed sum, each layer gets to attend over the outputs of previous layers, so the aggregation along depth becomes learned and input-dependent. In a sense you're doing for the depth dimension what attention already did for the sequence dimension. It's a very clean idea, and I think that's why it caught people's attention. It's elegant, and it has a natural interpretation.

My own thinking started from a slightly different place. I was less focused on making the depth connection fully attention-based. I was more interested in what the residual stream is actually doing as a communication channel, and in where the bottleneck is. So I cared about things like how much capacity the stream has, how information gets written and overwritten, and whether you can get most of the benefit with a lighter, more structural change rather than adding another attention mechanism over depth. Part of the motivation was practical. Anything you add on the depth axis has costs in memory, in kernel design, and in how it interacts with pipeline parallelism at scale. So I tended to ask, "What's the minimal change that fixes the dilution problem?"

So the way I'd put it: his approach is more expressive and more general. It lets the model decide everything about how to route across layers. Mine is more conservative and more about efficiency and the right inductive bias. I don't see them as competing so much as two points on a spectrum. Honestly, I think the interesting open question for the field is how much of that flexibility the model really uses. If you trained an attention-residual model and found that the learned patterns are fairly sparse or structured, that would suggest a cheaper fixed structure could capture most of it. If instead they're rich and highly input-dependent, that's a strong argument for going the full attention route. I'd really like to see that kind of analysis done carefully at scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes attention residuals as attending over previous layer outputs and Su Tinghao’s approach as a lighter structural change, but it never states that they mix hidden-state residuals versus attention projections, respectively.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the two approaches start from a very similar observation but go in different directions from there.

The observation we share is that the standard residual stream in a Transformer is kind of a blunt instrument. Every layer just adds its output to the same stream, with the same weight, and the model has no real way to say "this layer's contribution matters a lot for this token, and that layer's contribution matters very little." It's all summed up uniformly. Both of us looked at that and felt like something was being left on the table.

Where Guangyu went with it, as I understand his work, is to make the residual connection itself attentive. Instead of a plain sum, the current layer gets to look back over the outputs of previous layers and weight them, so the depth dimension starts to look a bit like the sequence dimension. It's an elegant idea, and the nice thing about it is that it's quite general. You can bolt it onto an existing architecture and it gives the model a learned routing over depth.

My approach is less about adding a mechanism and more about changing what flows through the stream. I was more interested in the question of what the residual is carrying, rather than how layers read from it. So we spent a lot of time on normalization and scaling of what each block writes back, and on separating the parts of the signal that need to persist across many layers from the parts that are really local. In practice that means fewer new parameters and less compute per layer than an attention-over-depth scheme, but it's also more opinionated. You have to make some structural commitments up front, and if those commitments are wrong for a given task, you don't get the flexibility that his approach would give you.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: his approach gives the model freedom and lets it learn how to use depth, and mine tries to encode a prior about how depth should be used and pays for that with less flexibility. I don't think one is strictly better. On small and mid-scale models I'd expect his to be easier to get working, because the model can figure things out on its own. At larger scale I'm somewhat more optimistic about ours, because every bit of per-layer overhead gets multiplied by a lot of layers, and a good prior starts to matter more than raw flexibility. But I'll be honest, that's a hypothesis, not something I'd claim we've proven. I'd actually really like to see someone combine the two, because I don't think they're in conflict at all.

r001.rationale: The response says Chen’s method attends over outputs from previous layers and describes Su’s method as changing the residual stream through normalization, scaling, and signal separation. It does not identify the distinction as mixing hidden-state residuals versus attention projections.

Without that context, I’d risk attributing a claim to him that he hasn’t made. Once we pin that down, we can compare the problem each approach addresses, how it works, and what the evidence shows.
